The unchecked rule guarantees the truncated value only when 'the value of the source operand is within the range of the destination type' (PDF p. 131, lines 1-4), so 255.75 -> byte falls to the unspecified-value branch (PDF p. 131, line 5), where the 7th edition guarantees 255 (PDF p. 155, lines 8-10). Every byte result, csc's 255 included, conforms at ISO-1, so no program can observe the difference; the 7th edition rows asserting the truncated value at such edges must not be asserted at ISO-1.

'Otherwise, the result of the conversion is an unspecified value of the destination type' (PDF p. 131, line 5) covers every source outside the range as tested before rounding (PDF p. 131, line 2), including fractional edges such as 255.75 -> byte that the 7th edition maps to 255 (PDF p. 155, lines 8-12). Since any destination value conforms and the conversion succeeds in both editions, no ISO-1 program can observe the difference; NaN and infinities give an unspecified value in both.

At ISO-1, System.ValueType storage = new Parcel(53); for a struct, and System.Enum storage = Signal.Ready; and System.ValueType storage = Signal.Ready; for an enum, are compile-time errors (no implicit conversion exists); the object-endpoint controls compile and print OK.

At ISO-1, Parcel result = (Parcel)storage; with storage of type System.ValueType, and (Signal)storage from System.Enum or System.ValueType, are compile-time errors; the setup casts through object are valid at ISO-1, and the object-source controls compile and print OK.

At ISO-1, unboxing a null object reference or a null interface reference to a value type throws System.InvalidCastException, so both null probes print INVALID (csc's hosted runtime prints NULL, a runtime departure); the wrong-box controls print INVALID at both levels.

At ISO-1, System.Collections.IList view = new int[0]; (likewise ICollection and IEnumerable) is a compile-time error; converting through (System.Array) first compiles and prints OK 0, and the conversion to System.ICloneable stays valid.
At ISO-1, System.ICloneable a = new int[0]; and System.ICloneable d = new Signal(Notify); must compile and run (printing OK 0); this is an acceptance test, since the bullet grants a conversion.

In a checked context, converting a non-constant double 255.75 (and likewise -0.75) to byte throws System.OverflowException at ISO-1; the controls 254.75 -> 254 and 257.0 -> OverflowException hold in both editions. The .NET runtime returns 255 and 0 at both levels, so the case is a recorded hosted-runtime departure.

The same test as ed1-13.2.1-030: at ISO-1 a checked conversion of a non-constant double 255.75 or -0.75 to byte throws System.OverflowException, where the runtime returns 255 and 0 (hosted-runtime departure).
